content.text: Journeying east in search of Sita, Rama and Lakshman came to the hermitage of the aged ascetic woman Savari (Shabari), deep in the wood near Pampa. She rose to greet them with hands upraised, bowed low, washed their feet, and offered them water — a lifetime's devotion arriving, at last, at the moment she had waited for.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

content.text: Shabari told Rama that her own teachers, great saints, had ascended to heaven from that very grove, but had left her a prophecy before they departed: 'In this pure grove, O devotee, Prince Rama soon will visit thee. When he and Lakshman seek this shade, be to thy guests all honour paid. Him shalt thou see, and pass away to those blest worlds which ne'er decay.' She had kept fruit gathered from every tree on Pampa's shore in store for this exact visit.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

content.text: Rama addressed her first not with a demand but with concern for her spiritual well-being: 'I trust no cares invade thy peace, while holy works and zeal increase; that thou content with scanty food all touch of ire hast long subdued; that all thy vows are well maintained... that reverence of the saints who taught the faithful heart due fruit has brought.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

content.text: Shabari answered that meeting Rama was itself the fruit of all her penance: 'My penance' meed this day I see complete, my lord, in meeting thee. This day the fruit of birth I gain, nor have I served the saints in vain... I feel, great lord, thy gentle eye my earthly spirit purify.' She then led the brothers through the grove, showing them the altars, lakes, and relics of the saints she had served for years.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

content.text: Having completed her long vigil of waiting and service, Shabari asked Rama's leave to end her life and join her departed teachers: 'Permit thy servant, lord, I pray, to cast this mortal shell away, for I would dwell, this life resigned, with those great saints of lofty mind, whom I within this holy shade with reverential care obeyed.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

content.text: Rama granted her wish simply and with respect: 'Go, lady, where thou fain wouldst be, O thou who well hast honoured me.' Shabari then resigned her body to flame and rose to heaven 'like the fire that burns and glows,' in celestial garments, 'bright with celestial gems,' attaining the sphere reserved for saints of the purest devotion.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

content.text: Shabari's episode is treasured in the bhakti tradition as proof that devotion, patience, and simple hospitality — offered by someone with no scriptural learning or high birth, only unwavering faith — earns the same divine regard as the greatest penance. Her fruit, given with love, is remembered as more precious than any ritual offering.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV
